daily_reality.summary: Judges preside over trials and hearings in local, state, and federal courts. They interpret law, assess evidence, make rulings, and sentence defendants. Heavy caseloads, complex legal analysis, and the weight of consequential decisions define the role.
typical_tasks: Presiding over trials, hearings, and motions
Reviewing legal briefs, motions, and case files
Making rulings on procedural and evidentiary matters
Conducting pretrial conferences and settlement discussions
Supervising law clerks and court staff
Participating in judicial conferences and continuing education
key_documents: Legal briefs and motions from attorneys

deadlines.motions_rulings: Varies — some require same-day rulings, others weeks to months
deadlines.opinion_writing: No strict deadlines for most courts, but judges tracked on pending caseload
deadlines.speedy_trial_act: 70 days from indictment to trial start (federal criminal cases)

daily_reality.seasonality: Court schedules follow terms. Federal courts operate year-round with recess periods. State courts may follow school-year-like schedules. Summer often lighter for filings.

regulatory.summary: Federal judges appointed under Article III of the Constitution with life tenure. Federal magistrate judges appointed by district judges for 8-year renewable terms. State judges elected or appointed per state constitution. Mandatory retirement ages vary (65-75). Judicial ethics governed by Code of Conduct for US Judges.

key_laws.name: U.S. Constitution Article III
key_laws.description: Establishes federal judiciary, provides life tenure for Article III judges

key_laws.name: 28 U.S.C. Chapter 43 — United States Magistrate Judges
key_laws.description: Authorizes appointment of federal magistrate judges

key_laws.name: Code of Conduct for United States Judges
State constitutional and statutory provisions
key_laws.description: Each state defines judicial selection, tenure, and retirement

requirements: Juris Doctor (J.D.) degree from ABA-accredited law school
Bar membership in at least one jurisdiction
Federal judges: nominated by President, confirmed by Senate (Article III)
Federal magistrates: appointed by district judges, bar membership required
State judges: elected or appointed per state constitution

regulatory.recent_changes: Immigration court system lost ~25% of judges in 2025-2026 due to firings and resignations. Federal judicial salary debates continue. Growing use of remote/hybrid courtroom technology post-pandemic.

tools.summary: Legal research databases, case management systems, courtroom technology, and opinion-writing tools. Remote hearing technology expanded post-pandemic.

primary_tools.name: Westlaw / LexisNexis
primary_tools.description: Primary legal research databases for case law, statutes, and secondary sources

primary_tools.name: CM/ECF (Case Management / Electronic Case Files)
primary_tools.description: Federal court electronic filing and case management system

primary_tools.name: PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records)
primary_tools.description: Public access system for federal court records

primary_tools.name: Courtroom technology
primary_tools.description: Video display systems, evidence presentation, audio recording

primary_tools.name: Video conferencing platforms
primary_tools.description: Zoom for Government, Microsoft Teams for remote hearings

secondary_tools: Word processing for opinion drafting (Word, WordPerfect in some courts)
pain_points: Paper-dependent processes in some state courts
Cybersecurity concerns with sensitive case data

terminology.summary: Legal and judicial terminology spanning procedural, substantive, and administrative court language.

terms.bench: The judge's seat in the courtroom; also the judiciary collectively
terms.chambers: Judge's private office where non-public work occurs
terms.en banc: Full appellate court hearing (all judges, not just a panel)
terms.recusal: Judge's withdrawal from a case due to conflict of interest
terms.sua sponte: Action taken by the court on its own initiative
terms.in camera: Private review by judge, not in open court
terms.bench trial: Trial decided by judge without jury
terms.dissent: Judge's written disagreement with the majority opinion
terms.concurrence: Agreement with the outcome but for different reasons
terms.remand: Sending a case back to a lower court
terms.stay: Court order pausing proceedings or enforcement
terms.magistrate: Judicial officer handling pretrial matters, minor offenses
terms.Article III judge: Federal judge with life tenure under the Constitution
terms.senior status: Semi-retired federal judge with reduced caseload

career_psychology.summary: Pinnacle of legal career. Median salary $156,210 (BLS); federal district judges earn $246,300. Enormous responsibility and isolation. Burnout is real: heavy caseloads, traumatic cases, and professional isolation. Mandatory retirement ages 65-75 in many jurisdictions.
career_path: Bar admission and legal practice (10-20+ years)
Build reputation in specific area of law
Judicial clerkship experience (early career, highly valued)
State appellate court / federal magistrate judge
Federal district court judge / state supreme court
Federal circuit court judge / U.S. Supreme Court
fears: Making a wrong decision affecting someone's life or liberty
Public scrutiny and politicization of judicial decisions
Personal safety threats from disgruntled litigants
Professional isolation and loneliness of the bench
Compassion fatigue from difficult cases (family, criminal)
motivation: Serving justice and upholding the rule of law
Intellectual challenge of complex legal analysis
Prestige and respect of judicial office
Public service at the highest level
burnout_factors: Exposure to traumatic cases and evidence
Professional isolation — few peers to confide in
Limited management support in some jurisdictions

community.summary: Professional community through the Federal Judicial Center, ABA Judicial Division, National Judicial College, and state judicial conferences. Collegial but inherently isolated profession.

market.summary: Very limited growth (1% projected 2024-2034). ~1,500 annual openings mostly from retirements. Highly competitive appointments. Immigration court crisis reducing judicial workforce. State court budgets vary widely.

demand_forecast.immigration_crisis: Immigration courts lost ~25% of judges in 2025-2026

market_trends: Very limited overall growth in judicial positions
Growing use of AI for legal research (not decision-making)
State court budget constraints affecting staffing
